newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Caltex Singapore's 100-oct petrol sparks concerns.
newsitem.headline: Caltex Singapore's 100-oct petrol sparks concerns.

text.p: U.S. major oil firm Caltex shot the first salvo in the war for Singapore's petrol market by launching a 100-octane unleaded grade, but immediately drew flak from rivals over its benefits and impact on health.
Caltex told a new briefing on Thursday, the higher octane number and the company's special additive Techron, would boost engine performance, enhance fuel economy and reduce emissions.
While rivals were quick to debunk the merits of the new petrol, companies such as Shell, Mobil Oil Singapore and Esso did not exclude introducing it at their own outlets if demand was good.
"We see no benefit to the consumer in introducing 100 Ron (octane)," Mobil Oil Singapore's spokeswoman said in response to a Reuter query.
"It is very much a marketing driven exercise that increases product costs, which will ultimately be passed on to consumers, if the industry went down that route, due to competitive pressure."
The octane level determines the ability of the petrol to ignite. The higher the octane level the easier it is to ignite the petrol.
But higher octane levels require more benzene additive, the material that has raised health concerns.

Earlier this week the Journal of the National Cancer Institute reported in the United States that a study of 75,000 Chinese workers showed benzene was found to increase the risk of leukaemia and other blood disorders.
However, the the Journal said questions remained concerning the link between the level of exposure and the level of risk.
Roger Organ, manager of Caltex's product engineering department said the 100-octane grade contains four to five percent benzene -- a level deemed safe by the industry.

Caltex's new petrol will replace its 98-octane unleaded grade at the pumps, making Singapore the first Asian country outside Japan to use the higher grade, Laurence Evans, Caltex Singapore's general manager for marketing said.

Evans said Caltex hoped the petrol would help the company expand market share, although he declined to say what level market share was now. Singapore's petrol market is worth more than S$100 million per month.
"It will cost more to produce the 100-octane gasoline but we are confident a sharp increase in our sales in the next few months will offset that extra cost," Organ said.
Evans did not discount the possibility of higher prices in three to six months depending on demand and production costs.
A Shell Singapore spokeswoman said 98 octane petrol is already one of the world's highest. She said there were cost and environmental issues that should be considered.

"Through extensive market research and research into fuels technology, as well as our active participation as a fuels/oils supplier in Formula One racing, we believe that the fuels preferences and needs of motorists in Singapore cannot be satisfied simply by increasing octane levels," she told Reuters.
While Shell said the 100-octane grade has been tried unsuccesfully elsewhere, such as in Japan, Caltex said about 18 percent of motorists there use it.
One Japanese source said the grade produces a good profit margins for refiners, so Japanese companies are trying to raise production.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3084)
